title: The MBIST controller
summary: The controller turns a March test into a sequence of commands — address, data, read or write — one per clock. It can be a fixed state machine for one algorithm, or a small programmable engine that runs any algorithm loaded into it.
objectives: Describe a March test as three nested loops and map them to counters.
Sketch a hard-wired controller for a given March test.
Write a simple March test as a microcode program.

subsections.title: A March test as nested loops

steps.title: Elements
steps.md: The outer loop walks through the **elements** of the test — an **element counter**.

steps.title: Addresses
steps.md: For each element, the middle loop walks through all **addresses** in the element's order — the **address counter** of Topic 3.

steps.title: Operations
steps.md: For each address, the inner loop runs the element's **operations** — an **operation counter**. Each operation is one memory access: write data, or read and compare.

steps.title: Done
steps.md: When the last operation of the last address of the last element is finished, the controller raises **done**; **pass** is 1 if no compare failed.

blocks.md: For one fixed algorithm the loops can be unrolled into a **state machine**. Each state issues one operation; the address counter and the *last* flag decide whether to stay in the element or move to the next. For MATS+ = {⇕(w0); ⇑(r0, w1); ⇓(r1, w0)}:

steps.title: Start and M0
steps.md: *start* leaves IDLE. **M0_W** writes 0 and stays until the last address.

steps.title: M1
steps.md: **M1_R** reads 0, **M1_W** writes 1, and the pair repeats going up until the last address.

steps.title: M2
steps.md: **M2_R** reads 1, **M2_W** writes 0, going down until address 0.

steps.title: Done
steps.md: **DONE** raises *done*; when *start* is released the controller returns to IDLE.

rows: M0_W — or M1_R after the last address (load 0)
M1_R — or M2_R after the last address (load N−1)
blocks.caption: A hard-wired MATS+ controller: one state per operation

blocks.title: Small, fast — and fixed
blocks.md: A hard-wired controller is a handful of flip-flops and gates and runs easily at speed. But the algorithm is frozen in silicon. Many chips include **a few** hard-wired algorithms (for example a production test and a short power-on test) and select one through IJTAG.
A **programmable** controller stores the algorithm as a short **program** in registers that are loaded through IJTAG. Each instruction describes one March element:

rows: up to k operations, each read/write + 0/1
blocks.caption: One microcode instruction = one March element

steps.title: Instruction 0: ⇕(w0)
steps.md: The program counter (PC) points to instruction 0. The address generator counts through all addresses, the sequencer issues one **w0** per address.

steps.title: Instruction 1: ⇑(r0, w1)
steps.md: Load 0, count up; at every address **r0** then **w1**.

steps.title: Instruction 2: ⇑(r1, w0)
steps.md: Up again with the opposite values.

steps.title: Instruction 5: ⇕(r0)
steps.md: The final read. This instruction has *last* = 1, so the controller raises **done** afterwards.

blocks.prompt: Practice: put the instructions of a MATS++ program {⇕(w0); ⇑(r0, w1); ⇓(r1, w0, r0)} in order.

tabs.label: Hard-wired
tabs.md:
**+** smallest area, simplest timing.

**−** only the algorithms chosen at design time. If silicon shows a new fault type, nothing can be changed.

tabs.label: Programmable
tabs.md:
**+** any March-type algorithm, loaded after the chip is made; different tests for production, power-on and diagnosis.

**−** more area (instruction registers, decoding), longer setup through IJTAG.

tabs.label: In practice
tabs.md: Commercial MBIST generators offer both and mix them: a library of built-in algorithms selectable at run time, plus an optional programmable mode for new algorithms. The engineer chooses per controller, depending on how critical the memories are.

questions.text: Order the loops of a March test from outermost to innermost.
Which counter decides when a March element is finished?
options: The address counter reaching the last address of the element's order

questions.text: In the hard-wired MATS+ controller, how many states issue memory operations?
In the programmable controller, what does one instruction describe?
options: One March element: order, operations, background

questions.text: What are advantages of a programmable controller? Select **all** correct answers.
options: A new algorithm can be used after the chip is made.
Different tests can be run for production, power-on and diagnosis.
It is always smaller than a hard-wired controller.
It needs no test access port.

questions.text: A chip may contain a few hard-wired algorithms and select one of them through IJTAG.
